M. pneumoniae is thought to respond to macrolides, tetracyclines, or quinolones, although data from placebo-controlled clinical trials are lacking. B

Recommendations for treatment of CAP in otherwise healthy outpatients is with amoxicillin A or doxycycline B . No clear benefit for adults or children has been demonstrated with use of antibiotics providing coverage for atypical pathogens compared with those that do not. B

background.definition: Mycoplasma, a mucosal bacterium without cell walls, is one of the organisms responsible for causing CAP. In addition to pneumonia, mycoplasma can exacerbate existing pulmonary disease and cause extrapulmonary complications.

list.listitem: Center for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that 2 million cases of M pneumoniae infections occur annually including between 1 and 10 in every 50 cases of CAP.
Age younger than 5 years: 30 to 45/1000 persons/year.
Ages 5 to 9 years: 16 to 20/1000 persons/year.
Ages 9 to 15 years: 9 to 12/1000 persons/year.
Age older than 15 years: 12/1000/persons/year.
Up to 90% of mycoplasma infections are seen in patients between the ages of 5 and 15 years; it generally does not cause serious disease.
M. pneumoniae accounted for 15% of CAP in a study of Canadian emergency departments, and 14% in a series of 184 hospitalized children.
Twenty percent of 12,025 hospitalized children with a respiratory tract infection (RTI) had mycoplasma infection.

In a prospective study conducted in 2010 to 2012, of 2222 children hospitalized with radiographic evidence of pneumonia, a nasopharyngeal or oropharyngeal swab, and an additional diagnostic specimen available, 8% had M. pneumoniae detected. Mycoplasma was found more often among children age 5 years or older than among younger children (19% vs. 3%).

Among 3834 patients hospitalized with COVID-19 from 30 studies, 7% had a bacterial co-infection (95% CI 3-12%, I2=92.2%), most commonly with M. pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Haemophilus influenzae.
M. pneumoniae is a frequent cause of outbreaks of respiratory disease in institutional or community settings.
M. pneumoniae may play a role in causing acute exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
There is a positive association between M. pneumoniae infection determined by IgM serology and childhood asthma (OR 3.13, 95% CI 1.78-5.48).
In one case series during an outbreak of Stevens-Johnson syndrome in a children’s hospital in Colorado, 5 of the 8 children had mycoplasma pneumonia based on polymerase chain reaction (PCR).
M. pneumoniae and other mycoplasma species.
Risk factors include smoking and reduced IgG levels, which increase the risk of acquiring M. pneumoniae during an outbreak.

In the large pediatric cohort of hospitalized children with RTI, a higher percentage of children with mycoplasma infection had the P1 gene, a key adhesion gene for mycoplasma. Several susceptibility genes have been identified among Chinese children.

Infection is primarily spread by aerosolized droplets from contaminated sputum and secretions. Due to its lack of a cell wall, M. pneumoniae is extremely susceptible to desiccation so droplet transmission from person to person only occurs through close contact.
Mycoplasma adheres to respiratory cells. Parasitized cells sustain local injury, resulting in loss of cilia and local inflammation leading to RTI.
Mycoplasmas lack a cell wall and are inherently resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics.
M. pneumoniae accounts for approximately 15% of CAPs. B

Adults with mycoplasma pneumonia tend to be younger and are more likely to have a nonproductive cough and less likely to have rhinitis. C Children with CAP are more likely to have mycoplasma pneumonia if they are over age 4 years, have nonproductive cough and associated chest pain and fever duration over one week. C
A prediction rule based on age and duration of fever helps to identify children with pneumonia at increased risk for mycoplasma pneumonia. C

Differential.Differential_Name: Other less common causes of RTI

list.listitem: No single finding is pathognomonic for the diagnosis of CAP due to mycoplasma disease.

Among children with CAP, the presence of chest pain more than doubles the probability of M. pneumoniae. Absence of wheezing was also a diagnostic indicator but was not of sufficient diagnostic value to guide empirical macrolide treatment.

An accumulation of findings increases the probability of pneumonia. For example, a patient from a high-risk setting with a presentation that includes acute cough, fever, tachycardia, and crackles on chest examination has a revised probability of 60%.

In a series of 106 patients, 12 of whom had mycoplasma, patients with mycoplasma infection tended to be younger (43 vs. 51 years), were more likely to have a nonproductive cough (42% vs. 17%), and had less rhinitis (8% vs. 62%).

Other symptoms thought to be more common in adults with CAP due to mycoplasma include confusion, myalgias, ear pain, diarrhea, erythema multiforme, nonexudative pharyngitis, pericarditis, myocarditis, and heart block.

M. pneumoniae is an uncommon cause of encephalitis. In a series of 58 cases, 76% had flulike illness prior to onset of neurologic symptoms. A mononuclear pleocytosis was seen in the CSF and imaging abnormalities were identified in about one-third of these children. lists other extrapulmonary manifestations.

Order a CXR for any patient who presents with a likelihood of CAP. Although this is standard care, a Cochrane review of 2 trials failed to show that a CXR improved outcome in outpatients with acute lower RTI.

An elevated procalcitonin level differentiates bacterial from viral pneumonia but is expensive and not required routinely. In an RCT of a protocol for CAP based on procalcitonin level versus standard care, there were similar rates of adverse outcomes with fewer days of antibiotics (5.7 vs. 8.7 days for standard care).

Patients with CAP caused by mycoplasma are more likely to have an elevated C-reactive protein (CRP; 83% vs. 49%) or erythromycin sedimentation rate (ESR; 100% vs. 58%). The National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE) recommends obtaining a CRP if, after clinical assessment, a diagnosis of pneumonia has not been made and it is not clear whether antibiotics should be prescribed. Antibiotic therapy should be offered if the concentration is greater than 100 mg/L.

Real-time PCR tests have been developed that have good sensitivity and specificity for detection of M. pneumoniae.
However, these are not widely available for clinical point-of-care use.

Based on a meta-analysis, commercial PCR tests have high specificity but insufficient sensitivity (0.62, 95% CI, 0.45-0.76) to replace serology for accurate diagnosis. A positive PCR result can be due to colonization vs. infection.

Paired serology (IgM, IgG) against M. pneumoniae offers definitive diagnosis, but requires between 4 and 8 weeks to complete with several visits needed to collect acute and convalescent sera specimens. IgM titers in the acute phase can remain high for months, so IgM alone is not useful for diagnosis.

In a study comparing the performance of serology and PCR in 491 children with and 61 children without CAP, investigators found a positive test for M. pneumoniae (PCR and/or paired serology or both) in 13.9% with CAP and a positive PCR for M. pneumoniae in 3.3% of children without CAP. Of the children with CAP, 10.3% were positive by multiplex PCR (Seeplex-Seegen), 6.7% exhibited quadrupled titers (22 for IgG, 6 for IgM and 5 for both), and both tests were positive in 2.8% of cases. Interestingly, 32% of children with CAP and 38.3% of healthy children had IgM titers >11.
With respect to serologic assays used for diagnosis, greater standardization is needed, particularly for IgG determination. An immunoblotting approach may improve test characteristics.

In a study of 453 patients with symptoms of pneumonia in India, 52 (11.4%) were positive for IgM antibodies, 17 were positive by culture, and seven tested positive by PCR (P1 gene). The authors concluded that all three methods may be required for accurate diagnosis. Culture, however, is time consuming, may take weeks to obtain and isolate organisms, and requires specialized reference laboratories.

Sputum appears to be the preferred specimen over nasopharyngeal swab for simultaneous detection of M. pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, and Legionella pneumophila using multiplex PCR in patients with CAP. In another study of hospitalized children with pneumonia, PCR from bronchoalveolar lavage and nasopharyngeal aspirate specimens were similar in diagnostic parameters.

A newer test using a loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) assay, completed in 60 minutes, had high sensitivity and specificity for mycoplasma pneumonia detection that was not inferior to PCR. In a case series of children with lower RTI, oropharyngeal loop-mediated isothermal amplification had 100% sensitivity and specificity compared with PCR testing.

A CRISPR-Cas12b-based detection platform has been developed using recombinase polymerase amplification for amplifying the community-acquired respiratory distress syndrome toxin gene of M. pneumoniae strains. This test appears to improve sensitivity for detection of M. pneumoniae.

An automatic gene analyzer that combines amplification with PCR and the quenching probe method to specify the gene and macrolide-resistant mutations simultaneously (Smart Gene) has been developed in Japan that has high concordance with real-time PCR.
Bronchoscopic imaging may have a role in diagnosis of children with refractory mycoplasma pneumonia.
A prediction rule can help identify the likelihood of M. pneumoniae infection in children.

Points are assigned for age (0 for <6 months, 1 for 6 months to 2 years, 2 for >2-4 years, 3 for >4-7 years, and 5 for >10 years) and duration of fever in days (0 for <1, 1 for 1-3, 2 for 4-5, 3 for 6-7, 4 for 8-14, and 5 for >14 days).
The risk of mycoplasma pneumonia is low for children with a total of 0 to 3 points (2%), moderate for 4 to 5 points (7%), high for 6 to 7 points (28%), and very high for 8 to 10 points (65%).

Based on a systematic review of 20 studies including 5289 patients found that mean differences in CRP, LDH, and % neutrophils, and lung consolidation (OR 14.29, 95% CI 4.52-45.12) were predictive factors for refractory Mycoplasma pneumonia.
Suspect mycoplasma pneumonia in children and younger adults with nonproductive cough. However, diagnostic testing to confirm diagnosis using PCR or serial titers is not recommended.
Follow guidelines for management of CAP in adults and children.
Evidence regarding treatment has found no difference in outcomes between macrolides and nonmacrolides or macrolides and quinolones for patients with non-severe community-acquired pneumonia.

Recommended empiric CAP therapy for adult outpatients without comorbidities or risk factors for drug-resistant pathogens are amoxicillin ( A ) or doxycycline ( B ) per the 2019 American Thoracic Society and Infectious Diseases Society of America recommendations; these recommendations are based on low quality of evidence (QOE). Macrolide monotherapy (azithromycin or clarithromycin) for outpatients with CAP is an option in areas with pneumococcal resistance to macrolides that is lower than 25% (moderate QOE). B

The above guideline recommends a β-lactam (amoxicillin-clavulanate or cephalosporin) plus a macrolide ( A ; moderate QOE), a β-lactam plus doxycycline ( B ; low QOE), or monotherapy with a respiratory fluoroquinolone ( A ; moderate QOE) for CAP in adult outpatients with comorbidities; typical duration is 5-7 days.

Comparisons of regimens covering atypical bacteria with β-lactams generally do not show an advantage for β-lactams in patients with mycoplasma pneumonia, although they are recommended based on in vitro efficacy. High-quality studies are lacking. B
Give a fluoroquinolone to patients who have comorbidities, who fail initial treatment, or who have recently received antibiotics. C
Specific treatment recommendations, including inpatient therapy, are available in the chapter on community-acquired pneumonia.

Because an etiologic agent is identified in only 50% of patients with CAP, choose treatment on an empiric basis to cover likely pathogens. Initial choice of amoxicillin or doxycycline for a previously healthy adult patient with CAP is recommended by the 2019 Infectious Diseases Society of America/American Thoracic Society guidelines. Cochrane authors found insufficient evidence to draw any specific conclusions about the efficacy of antibiotics for Mycoplasma pneumonia in children, although one trial suggested that azithromycin may be efficacious. Quinolones and tetracyclines are contraindicated in children younger than 12 and 7 years, respectively. NICE recommends against prescribing quinolones to patients with low-severity CAP.

The 2019 guideline recommends a β-lactam (amoxicillin-clavulanate or cephalosporin) plus a macrolide, a β-lactam plus doxycycline, or monotherapy with a respiratory fluoroquinolone for CAP in adult outpatients with comorbidities for 5-7 days.

Studies have not found any differences among macrolides, tetracyclines, and quinolones for treatment of mycoplasma pneumonia. In fact, a meta-analysis of 18 studies comparing a β-lactam with a macrolide, fluoroquinolone, or ketolide found no difference in clinical cure rates for the 211 patients with mycoplasma and 115 with chlamydia pneumonia, but did find a benefit for those with legionella pneumonia. Similarly, a study comparing primary care treatment of lower RTI found no difference in outcomes between roxithromycin and amoxicillin, but only 1% of patients in this study had mycoplasma pneumonia. Authors of a Cochrane review also found no significant difference in the incidence of clinical failure on about days 10 to 14 between patients with acute lower respiratory tract infection treated with azithromycin vs. amoxicillin or amoxicillin/clavulanic acid.

Among children, a meta-analysis of 7 studies with 1491 children found insufficient evidence regarding antibiotics for lower RTI due to M. pneumoniae. They found no difference in clinical response between children receiving a macrolide and a nonmacrolide antibiotic.
Authors of a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs, found no significant differences between macrolides and fluoroquinolones for clinical failure rates in CAP associated with any atypical bacteria.

The CDC reports a prevalence of macrolide resistance in M. pneumoniae of about 10% in the United States, with regional variability. The most recent report on prevalence of resistance to macrolides for M. pneumoniae worldwide found macrolide-resistant was most common in Asia (63%, 95% CI 56-69%) with much lower rates in Europe, North America, South America and Oceania (3%, 8.6% [6, 11], 0% and 3.3%, respectively).
With respect to antibiotic resistance, investigators found a genotypic-resistance rate of 44.4% for macrolide-resistant M. pneumoniae among 903 pediatric patients with CAP.
Corticosteroids

The 2019 guidelines from the American Thoracic Society and the Infectious Diseases Society of America advise against adjunctive corticosteroid treatment except in patients who have other indications for their use such as asthma, COPD, or an autoimmune disease.

Outcomes of studies on corticosteroids for admitted patients with CAP are mixed. One RCT of 304 patients found that dexamethasone added to antibiotic treatment reduced length of stay (6.5 days [5.0-9.0] vs. 7.5 days [5.3-11.5]) but increased rates of hyperglycemia (44% vs. 23%, respectively). There were no differences in mortality or adverse events. Another RCT of 213 patients hospitalized with CAP found no differences between groups randomized to daily prednisolone vs. placebo on outcomes.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 13 Chinese RCTs comparing use of low- versus high-dose methylprednisolone in 1049 children with severe Mycoplasma pneumonia found high-dose significantly more effective than low-dose in clinical efficacy (RR 1.30, 95% CI 1.23, 1.38) with no significant difference in adverse events. In another meta-analysis of 12 studies including 1130 children, azithromycin combined with corticosteroid treatment improved clinical efficacy in refractory Mycoplasma pneumonia.

Based on a network meta-analysis of 130 RCTs, combination azithromycin and Chinese medicine (Reduning, Tanreqing, Xiyanping, or Yanhuning) was more effective than azithromycin alone, with Tabreqing demonstrating the best clinical efficacy.
Provide supportive care to all patients: hydration, nutritional support, antipyretics, and oxygen as needed.
Chest physiotherapy is not helpful in children with pneumonia and may provoke symptoms.
Guidelines recommend outpatient antibiotic treatment for a minimum of 5 days.
NICE recommends a 5-day course of a single antibiotic to patients with low-severity CAP and a 7 to 10 day course of antibiotic therapy for patients with moderate- or high-severity CAP.
A Cochrane review of 4 studies found three days of antibiotics as effective as 5 days in children aged 2 to 59 months with non-severe CAP.

Patients with CAP who have comorbid conditions should be evaluated using a validated prediction rule such as the Pneumonia Severity Index or CURB-65 to assess severity and identify need for hospitalization.
Patient demographic characteristics (eg, age), social circumstances (eg, homelessness) and clinician's judgment should be used to augment the prediction rule scoring.
Most cases of pneumonia caused by mycoplasma resolve within 2 weeks. B
Mycoplasma encephalitis has a high morbidity (34% with sequelae) and mortality (9%). B
Myocardial damage can occur; in one study, the median serum CK-MB concentration was significantly higher in children with mycoplasma pneumonia compared with those who were M. pneumoniae IgM negative.
Mycoplasma infection may exacerbate baseline asthma in children.
Encephalitis is the most common neurologic extrapulmonary occurrence in children.

Authors of a meta-analysis found no difference between macrolides and nonmacrolides for treatment of lower RTI in children due to mycoplasma; in most studies, however, investigators failed to identify children with M. pneumoniae. A single RCT reviewed by the Cochrane authors demonstrated improved cure rates at 1 month for azithromycin vs. no azithromycin (100% vs. 77%) among children with recurrent RTIs whose acute lower RTI was due to mycoplasma, chlamydia or both per PCR.

An older guideline recommends a macrolide as the empiric antibiotic for children older than 5 years with CAP and high-dose amoxicillin (80-90 mg/kg/d) for children between the ages of 60 days and 5 years.

In a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs with 2233 children, the authors found insufficient evidence to support or refute antibiotic treatment for children thought to have mycoplasma pneumonia (enrollment included children with any pneumonia). 4 of the 5 studies found no benefit but there was substantial study bias, difficulty interpreting testing modalities, and inability to correct for mixed infections or intervention timing.
In an RCT of children admitted with CAP, only those admitted with wheezing (on beta agonists) had a reduction in length of stay when given steroids.

feature.caption: Common Extrapulmonary Manifestations of Mycoplasma pneumoniae Infection.
feature.feature_body:
Organ System Complications of Mycoplasma
Gastroenterologic Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea
Central nervous system Encephalitis (in children), aseptic meningitis, cranial nerve palsies, Guillan-Barré syndrome
Dermatologic Erythematous maculopapular eruptions; mucocutaneous syndromes
Musculoskeletal Myalgias, arthralgias, polyarthropathy
Data from Waites KB, Talkington DF. Mycoplasma pneumoniae and its role as a human pathogen. Clin Microbiol Rev 2004;17:697-728; Cunha BA. The atypical pneumonias: clinical diagnosis and importance. Clin Microbiol Infect 2006;12(Suppl 3):12-24
